Source: Paul's addendum "Melange Annotated Bibliography — Addendum" (sha12 d09295bf5960), read in full (68 lines). The companion reviewer-annotation file _annots/d09295bf5960.json does not exist, so there are no reviewer comments or highlights to add. Entries are Paul's own annotations paraphrased, and citations are recorded as he wrote them; I did not verify them externally.

Overarching argument: the section extends the static influence-maximization entries (Kempe et al. 2003; Nemhauser-Wolsey-Fisher 1978, covered elsewhere) into a dynamic regime organized in three tiers that mirror the Melange architecture. Tier 1 is one-shot greedy, which is static and submodular and gives the 1-1/e (about 63%) bound. Tier 2 is adaptive greedy, the bridge: a subordinate routine that replans within a campaign as intelligence arrives, with a survival guarantee (Golovin-Krause; CELF makes it computationally practical). Tier 3 is the RL envelope, where a learned outer policy handles cross-campaign compounding, where no greedy guarantee reaches.

Unifying claim: the inner static problem is submodular, the inner sequential problem is adaptive submodular, and the full cross-campaign problem is non-submodular. Paul asserts that RL4CCIM confirms the last point for complex contagion, and that the non-submodular regime is where the durable competitive moat lives.

Systems linked: the operational layer (D* Lite / LPA*, incremental replanning) maps to adaptive submodularity; the strategic layer (MCTS and the orienteering "reach-while-collecting" frame) maps to the RL-IM sequential, long-horizon problem; the political-capital budget maps to GCOMB's budget constraint; the subordinate greedy routine feeds the outer MDP through marginal-influence shaping rewards.

Research questions and implicit hypotheses: (a) whether coalition formation in Congress is a complex contagion (a fence-sitter commits only once enough allies have), which Paul calls "plausibly" true and which would place Melange outside the submodular regime; (b) whether relationship and persuasion costs, unknown a priori, can be learned by probing (Kamarthi); (c) whether lobbying commitment that is probabilistic rather than guaranteed (Chen 2021) changes the seeding policy.

Stated gaps and caveats in the addendum: adaptive submodularity presumes exact expected spread, which is NP-hard in general, and this is the stated reason Paul still drifts toward learned methods. The frontier paragraph says the four anchored RL entries are "sufficient"; the section in fact anchors seven RL-IM entries plus foundations, so that sentence is loosely worded. The frontier work (MaDGNN) is named without authors or DOI and is not anchored. The Golovin entry's "first to study influence maximization under the adaptive model" is Paul's priority claim and is unverified here.

Structure: three tiers mirror the Melange architecture. One-shot greedy (static, submodular, about 63% bound) gives way to adaptive greedy (within-campaign replanning, survival guarantee via adaptive submodularity and CELF lazy evaluation), which gives way to the RL envelope (cross-campaign compounding, no greedy guarantee).

Unifying claim: inner static problem is submodular; inner sequential problem is adaptive submodular; full cross-campaign problem is non-submodular (Paul says RL4CCIM confirms this for complex contagion). He locates the durable competitive moat in the non-submodular regime.

Syntheses across works: Golovin-Krause and CELF give the adaptive greedy bridge; Ng et al. 1999 licenses marginal-influence shaping so greedy feeds the outer MDP; Sutton-Barto and Watkins supply the MDP and Q-learning machinery; Khalil -> GCOMB -> Kamarthi -> Chen 2021 -> Chen 2023 form a progression from learned construction, to budget-scale, to unknown networks, to contingent commitment, to complex contagion.

Mapping to Melange components: operational layer (D* Lite / LPA*) = adaptive greedy; strategic layer (MCTS, orienteering reach-while-collecting) = RL-IM sequential long-horizon decisions; political-capital budget = GCOMB budget constraint; relationship/persuasion cost discovery = Kamarthi probing; coalition formation = complex contagion hypothesis.

Research questions Paul poses implicitly: is congressional coalition formation a complex contagion (untested, stated as plausible); can unknown relationship costs be learned by probing; does probabilistic lobbying commitment change optimal seeding; which early investments deserve credit when a vote flips (temporal credit assignment).

Stated gaps and caveats: adaptive submodularity presumes exact expected spread, which is NP-hard in general (stated reason he drifts toward learned methods); frontier work is named without authors or DOI and not anchored; the 'four anchored entries sufficient' sentence is inconsistent with the seven RL-IM entries actually anchored.

Cross-references outside this section that the addendum relies on but does not anchor here: Kempe et al. 2003 and Nemhauser-Wolsey-Fisher 1978 (static IM baseline, covered in the main bibliography); D* Lite and LPA* (operational layer); MCTS and orienteering (strategic layer).

Verification status: citations and arXiv IDs are recorded as Paul wrote them and were not checked against external sources. Priority claims (Golovin-Krause as first adaptive IM study; RL4CCIM as the 'clearest validation') are his assertions.

Source: "Machine Learning & Sentiment Analysis - Annotated Bibliography" (sha12 b0774147a262), read in full from C:\Users\pgoff\Documents\research\annotations\. The sidecar C:\Users\pgoff\Documents\research\_annots\b0774147a262.json does not exist, so there are no reviewer comments or highlights to fold in. The document lists 8 cited works. Only 4 (Birkenmaier and Lechner; Kim et al.; Peng et al.; Ramey et al.) have annotation text. The other 4 (Alkazzi and Okumura; Joo and Steinert-Threlkeld; Taherdoost and Madanchian; Steinert-Threlkeld) are citation-only.

Overarching argument: Paul treats machine learning and NLP applied to public political text (congressional floor speech, public statements, lobbying filings) as a way to produce actor-level attributes (personality traits, policy positions, emotion) that can be placed on nodes of a social-network-analysis graph. The purpose he names is political intelligence: lobbying strategy, industry alignment, and how to pitch policy to a specific member of Congress.

Research questions and gaps Paul states:
1. Conversion step. Birkenmaier and Lechner, Peng et al., and Ramey et al. each say the pipeline does not specify how a model's output becomes a graph node or vector. This is the most repeated gap in the document.
2. Ambiguity. Birkenmaier and Lechner say the method does not separate ambiguous statements.
3. Conflict. Kim et al. do not show inter-industry conflict over a specific bill, which Paul says matters for political intelligence.
4. Temporal lag. Kim et al. are reactive, not predictive, because filing reports lag current positions.
5. Model limits. Peng et al. say long-distance dependency is the main obstacle for most emotion models; stacking reduces but does not remove it.
6. Venue coverage. Ramey et al. offer no pipeline for textual venues beyond their own, and Paul says a framework for contextual or auditory constraints is also needed.

Synthesis: Birkenmaier and Lechner and Ramey et al. both concern personality measurement from speech or text, with Ramey et al. as the older foundation and Birkenmaier and Lechner as the newer, codebook-backed method. Kim et al. and Birkenmaier and Lechner both concern the actor-to-graph link. Peng et al. supplies the model landscape that the other two would run on.

Self-declared gap: Paul says his own technical grounding is not yet sufficient for Peng et al. and plans a second reading after more background.

Path-finding link: Alkazzi and Okumura is the only multi-agent path-finding item. Paul wrote no annotation for it, so any link to Melange path-finding is not in his words.

paul_notes.doc: Paul's annotation file (sha12 4b53f8cc145e) is short: six cited works, each with a citation line and a commentary paragraph, and no reviewer comments. The file does not name Moneyball, Mentat, Terrier, or path-finding; the only system-facing language is "social network analysis vector graph" and "future allocation models". Taken together, the commentary argues four things. Lobbying pays: firms that lobby for beneficial legislation see large returns (Alexander), lobbying lifts revenue and concentration (Huneeus and Kim; Bickmore), with the revenue gain partly at the expense of the wider economy. Access and influence are bought through donations, and the effect is strongest for committee-related activity and fades unless renewed (Kim, In Song et al.). Information is filtered by staffers' ideology, so advocacy should be routed through ideologically aligned think tanks; Paul proposes treating think-tank funding like venture capital in allocation models. Existing position-mapping pipelines (Kim, Jiseon et al.) are useful for SNA but reactive and blind to inter-industry conflict over a bill, which Paul calls vital for political intelligence. The implied research questions are: does lobbying pay, and for whom (size, industry); do donations buy legislative involvement, and how durable is it; does the information source matter; and can position data be used predictively. Stated gaps: no predictive capability, no conflict detection, and no link yet from these findings to specific Melange, Moneyball, or Mentat components.

paul_notes.doc:
Source read in full: C:\Users\pgoff\Documents\research\_text\bc2c16a312a8.txt (282 lines, sha12 bc2c16a312a8). The matching annotation file C:\Users\pgoff\Documents\research\_annots\bc2c16a312a8.json does not exist, so Paul's annotations are the in-text parentheticals and sentences that discuss each work. Where a work has none, the entry says so and the verbatim anchor is the reference-list line. Folder labels below are my grouping, not taken from any file. System links are not stated in the document, so system_links is empty throughout.

Overarching argument: Paul asks whether an industry's year-over-year economic performance predicts its federal political spending (campaign contributions and lobbying), and whether expected partisan control of Congress shapes the amount and partisan direction of that spending. Five initial sectors: commercial banks, credit unions, life insurance, auto manufacturing, crypto (crypto analyzed separately). Hypotheses: H1 deep pockets (positive growth effect); H1-alt distress (negative or asymmetric effect); H2 access-seeking (Republican share rises with expected Republican control); H3 stakes (total contributions rise with a toss-up); H4 lobbying tracks current control more than projected control.

Design synthesis: one distributed-lag model with prior-year and same-year growth (prior-year is the main test, for reverse-causality and timing reasons); pooled panel with sector fixed effects; log CPI-deflated dollars; within-sector z-scored growth; negative-growth indicator; lagged lobbying as a control (cites Kerr, Lincoln & Mishra 2014); projected control as probability of majority (Shift = P minus current majority; Tossup = 1 minus |2P minus 1|), with a directional RShare outcome; year fixed effects as the robustness alternative; wild cluster bootstrap for p-values with 5 clusters and Driscoll-Kraay SEs where year-level terms appear. Cox & Magar (1999) motivates the majority-status (not raw seat) measure.

Stated gaps and self-flagged limits: about 9 elections (2008-2024) so year-level politics variables have little leverage; 5 clusters make inference fragile; same-year growth may be caused by the spending; growth measures not comparable across sectors; OpenSecrets codes do not match NAICS and BEA aggregates banks with credit unions and life insurers with other carriers; regime changes (Citizens United and SpeechNow 2010, McCutcheon 2014, the 2008 LDA quarterly change, the 2024 CUNA-NAFCU merger); crypto donor concentration and Fairshake outside spending; unobserved 501(c) dark money and unregistered lobbying; correlational design only.

Open questions Paul asks (Section 8, 14 numbered): contribution timing (annual vs cycle); what counts as strategic spending; normalization by sector size; probability vs seat change; best historical P measure and odd-year handling; RShare vs alternatives; event study vs regression with about 9 elections; LDA measurement (in-house vs contract, trade associations, shadow lobbying, issue codes); quarterly lobbying; sign of performance-spending relation and anchoring papers (Grier, Munger & Roberts as a starting point); life insurance state regulation (McCarran-Ferguson); sector issue-salience control; estimator choice with lagged DV and few clusters; what reviewers would flag first.

Claims Paul marks for checking (not verified by this read, flag before relying on them): Cox & Magar's about $36,000 per member figure; Cook rating accuracy (about 94% Lean, 97% Likely, 100% Solid); OpenSecrets API discontinued April 15, 2025; Fairshake roughly $260 million over 2023-24; CUNA/NAFCU merger effective January 1, 2024; the six chamber flips (House 2010, 2018, 2022; Senate 2014, 2020, 2024). On the last, the Senate flip usually dated 2020 took effect in January 2021 after the Georgia runoffs, so the year may need a note. Also verify Kerr et al.'s persistence claim and the Cox & Magar corrigendum status.

Other items Paul cites that are not literature works (events and data, not entries): Dodd-Frank (2010), GENIUS Act (2025), McCarran-Ferguson Act, Citizens United, SpeechNow, McCutcheon, LDA reforms, OpenSecrets, DIME, FEC bulk data, LDA.gov API, Iowa Electronic Markets, Cook Political Report, 538 generic ballot, FRED, FDIC, NCUA, ACLI, NAIC, BEA, Fed G.17, CoinGecko/Coin Metrics, IBISWorld.

Those entries say so, and the verbatim anchor is the reference-list line or the in-text sentence. Takeaways marked 'My view, not Paul's' are my own inferences and should not be attributed to Paul.

Paul's three key arguments: (1) use the probability of majority control instead of raw seat change, because majority status carries access (Cox & Magar); (2) measure the directional outcome (RShare) separately from total dollars, because total dollars cannot show direction; (3) use actual growth only in estimation, with forecasts kept out of the growth variable to avoid look-ahead.

Syntheses across works: Cox & Magar and Snowberg et al. jointly support the projected-control design (value of majority status, and prediction markets as the ex-ante measure). Kerr et al. and de Figueiredo & Richter jointly support the lobbying specification and its persistence control. Grier et al. is the only work offered for the theory question (sign of the performance-spending relation).

Stated research gaps: the sign of the performance-spending relation (Q10); whether to add state data for life insurance (Q11); a sector-level issue-salience control (Q12); a better measure of P for odd years (Q5); and whether an event-study design would beat a regression with about 9 elections (Q7).

Verify before relying on: the $36,000 Cox & Magar figure; the Cook accuracy percentages; the OpenSecrets API discontinuation date; the Fairshake total; the CUNA/NAFCU merger date; and the list of six chamber flips. The Senate flip usually dated 2020 took effect in January 2021 after the Georgia runoffs, so the year may need a note.

No system links are stated in the document. The project is a separate sector-level political-economy design, not one of the Melange, Moneyball, Mentat, or Terrier systems, and the document does not connect it to them. Nothing was written to any repo, the brain vault, or the Project Brain.

The document is not a literature annotation file. It is Paul's DRAFT implementation/override specification for a "contact_plausibility" layer in fec/lobbying/ (dated 2026-08-27, revised 2026-08-28). Its "takeaways" on the cited works are therefore Paul's stated positions inside the spec, paraphrased. The works are cited only briefly, and no folder metadata is given for any of them.

Overarching arguments: (1) The existing structural join (build_dyad_bill_sets, every sponsor and cosponsor of every bill an org cites) answers "whose bills did this org lobby on," not "whom did this org plausibly contact." The new layer annotates that join and does not replace it. (2) Contacts are real and undisclosed; the disclosure carries no structured member field (LD-2 line 17 holds chamber/agency values only), so member signal must come from free text (covered positions, activity descriptions) and other sources. (3) Abstention is a first-class output, to avoid the argmax-always-answers defect Paul attributes to the LobbyView 2018 pipeline. (4) Inference must never be promoted to observation: every surface says "inferred contact plausibility," never "lobbied" or "contacted."

Research questions and gates: Can channels C1-C5 (revolving-door employment, dated committee venue, donation co-occurrence, serial activity, alignment/salience) carry a calibrated score? The fused feature budget is capped at 10 (H10). Fusion stays receipts-only until a gold set exists and one look is taken (H8). Open decisions for Paul: G1 LD-203 collector; G2 historical rosters for the 115th-117th Congresses; G3 gold-set adjudication ownership (flags that routing bulk labeling to Haiku 4.5 needs its own ruling); G4 prereg entry; G5 parser extension (byte-match proof required); G6 gold-set scope (Gate E1, likely underpowered on measured yield).

Syntheses across works: Paul treats the LobbyView lineage (2018 pipeline doc, Kim and Kunisky 2021 Political Analysis paper, 2025 arXiv paper) as one cautionary chain. Its failure mode is an undocumented inference asserted as capability. He keeps only the parts he can document and re-derives others with explicit rules (named committee relations, dated windows, monotonicity/no-look-ahead). He also uses the Kim and Kunisky contact prevalence figure as the motivation for the whole layer.

Stated gaps and open items: no gold labels exist yet (C6 named-target anchors are reserved as gold, not features). The 117th Congress roster is missing (G2). Inherited open items F23 (malformed concatenated bill key in the MBA 2024 index, inflating C4 counts) and F18 (88 duplicate filing_uuid rows) feed the layer's inputs. The LD-203 contributions endpoint is uncollected, so C3 is org-PAC only until G1. The arXiv 2025 paper and Stewart & Woon have no full bibliographic detail in the document. The companion file CONTACT_INFERENCE_EVALUATION.md is referenced but was not part of this read.

Other sources named in the spec (not works with takeaways, listed in the entries where relevant): congress-legislators GitHub repo (G2 option a), HSall_members.csv, BILLSTATUS, FEC derived CSVs, cosponsor_forecast.py, member_receptivity.json, data/stance artifacts.

doc_level_notes: Current conclusion (Sections 1, 5-7): the estimates do not establish that expected party gains reliably predict a larger share of campaign contributions, and do not support a validated next-calendar-year forecast. Seat-gain coefficients are positive but not significant (House p about 0.66, CR2 95% interval -2.49 to +2.96 points per 10 seats; Senate p about 0.59, interval -6.86 to +7.91 points). Both models have worse chronological error than carrying forward the previous cycle's share. The expected-control IEM result is not significant under election-cluster inference (House p 0.075 CR2, Senate 0.12 CR2).

Overarching argument: the 'missing forecast data' problem was a sample restriction, not an absence of data. The IEM workbooks cover 2002-2022 (including 2008 and 2010 under Democratic House control), and Crystal Ball seat calls run through 2024. The House 2020 failure comes from a rank-deficient training fold (RMajNow constant at 1 in 2012-2018, so 8 coefficients have rank 7). The handoff says to describe this as a design limitation, not a data shortage.

Methodological arguments: (a) PAC-plus-individual partisan shares cannot be read as absolute spending, because a higher Republican share can reflect falling Democratic giving, rising Republican giving, or both; (b) the checks are retrospective prediction diagnostics, not real-time forecasts, because test inputs include final pre-election calls and full-sample growth standardization; (c) the expected-seat-gain variable is seats, not a probability; (d) the sign of both estimates reverses under some election or industry omissions, so no dependable allocation rule follows.

Research questions: the original three analyses (contribution amount, partisan direction, lobbying). This handoff covers only the partisan-direction analysis, with control probability as the main predictor and expected seat change as a robustness check, kept separate. The brief's instruction not to search for significance is repeated throughout.

Syntheses across works: the IEM definitional caveat (2010 D-to-NR contracts are not pooled with modern OTHER-outcome markets) and the FEC reconciliation failure (67 of 80 chamber-party comparisons match, aggregate off by $164,489) both block the same inference, which is subtracting PAC dollars from combined totals to get individual giving.

Stated gaps (Section 8): (1) historical money/growth join for pre-2012 cycles; (2) forecast-event metadata (source, timing, settlement); (3) consistent Crystal Ball seat baselines, including a midpoint for two unassigned 2020 Georgia Senate races and unverified publication dates; (4) complete PAC/individual chamber split not yet validated (127 PAC pages archived, collection halted by 429s); (5) FEC/OpenSecrets reconciliation; (6) next-calendar-year alignment after the forecast cutoff; (7) donor-role and channel classification (individual giving is not employee giving; super PAC receipts are not independent expenditures).

doc_level_notes: Central argument: the study asks whether industries spend differently on politics when they have grown, are growing, or expect to grow. Two opposing mechanisms are kept open: better performance supplies more money, or weak performance or a weak forecast prompts spending to seek favorable policy. The sign is left to estimation.

Two kinds of forecast are kept distinct: predicted industry growth is the independent variable of direct interest (C3, L3), while predicted congressional control is a political control and a predictor of partisan direction.

Six core tests: contributions (C1 prior actual growth, C2 same-year actual growth, C3 predicted growth) and lobbying (L1, L2, L3). Actual-growth tests are associations. C3 and L3 are the tests that address the forecast directly. All six must be reported, including null, negative and inconclusive results.

Design: pooled multiple OLS with sector fixed effects, outcomes in millions of 2025 dollars, growth in percentage points. The plan argues pooling gives more information than fitting about 18 annual observations per sector separately, and it treats simple regression only as an illustration.

Extensions are kept separate: job-tier differences (Chief, Middle Management, Employee reference, with growth-by-tier interactions), chamber-specific Democratic share models, prior plus predicted growth together, and a logged-spending sensitivity check. Zero and negative net totals must not be dropped to make logs work.

Stated epistemic limits: the forecasts proxy public expectations, not firms' private expectations or whether a donor read the report. Results are to be read as associations consistent with a response to public forecasts, not causation. Effect size, uncertainty and consistency take priority over p-values.

Stated readiness gap: verified contribution years overlap the prepared congressional forecasts only in 2021-2022, which is too little annual variation to identify the full control specification. Earlier contributions and/or extended congressional forecasts are needed before the core models can be fitted. Adding sectors or tiers does not fix this.

Other gaps the plan names: life insurance, auto, Credit Arms, P&C and Telecom lobbying totals still need classification; Fintech lacks a comparable annual series; crypto has one verified forecast; Telecom wired, ISP and satellite archives are uncollected; the 2008 auto and life-insurance lagged-growth observations are incomplete.

works.title: Mapping the Political Personality (PoliPers): An Integrative Framework for Assessing Ideal and Actual Personality Profiles in Politicians (version 0.1)
works.summary:
PoliPers is a working paper (version 0.1, not peer reviewed) that builds a survey inventory of 15 politically relevant personality facets. Examples are Trust & Faith in Others, Compromise & Cooperativeness, Assertiveness & Will to Take Control, Empathy & Compassion, and Integrity & Honesty. Each facet is mapped to the Big Five, HEXACO, VIA, the Agency/Communion "Big Two" and the Aaldering-Vliegenthart leadership traits. The authors test it in four German samples: self-ratings (N=404), ideal-politician ratings (N=589) and crowd ratings of Trump and Merkel (N=211).

Reliability is uneven. Self-rating alphas run from .44 to .87, and Loyalty, Humility and Compromise all fall at or below .51. Assertiveness splits into two factors: the "power-hungry, claims leadership" item loads reversed in ideal ratings, and observer-rating alpha is .40. Observer ratings carry a large evaluative component. Empathy correlates with likeability at r=.70/.76 and Integrity with rated honesty at .70/.80. Rated facets also correlate with the rater's ideological proximity to the target, for example r=.46 between Integrity and proximity for Trump. The paper calls these "predictive validity", but all of them are concurrent associations measured on the same occasion.

The paper matters here because it is the upstream source of the two facet labels in Paul's agency/communion persona codebook (fec/members/agency_communion_llm.py), which feeds the receptivity layer at PERSONA_W 0.30. It does not test how personality affects response to pressure, lobbying, cosponsorship or votes. Its evidence therefore bears on how the persona construct is defined and on rater-bias risks. It gives no support to the susceptibility signs the engine assigns. It also supports two existing design choices: de-identifying text before LLM rating, and modeling halo as a method factor. Transfer is limited by the setting: German raters, two very prominent leaders, and the 2020-21 era.
works.question: How can political personality be assessed with a comprehensive, facet-level, contextualized, psychometrically validated inventory that works for (a) voters' ideal traits for politicians, (b) citizens' perceptions of actual politicians' traits, and (c) perceived self-other similarity between voters and politicians? (p.2, p.11-12)
works.method: Item construction from explicit facet definitions with two disambiguating trait words per item and balanced positive/negative keying (pp.21-22). 5-point agreement scale (Study 2, 3) and 1-5 scale for facet composites (Study 4). Composite facet scores are prorated means of 4-item scales (Dedication & Sacrifice uses 2 items). Factorial validity: principal components analysis of ipsatized items (centered on each respondent's mean to remove acquiescence) with Horn (1965) parallel analysis, 1,000 random draws, run in Stata fapara (pp.24-25, 28, 30). Reliability: Cronbach's alpha and composite reliability omega from a CFA congeneric model (Raykov, 1997), Stata sem/relicoef (pp.25, 28, 30). Convergent validity: correlations of facet composites with BFI-2-XS domain scores and a three-item Machiavellianism scale (Study 2, Table 3); Study 4 correlations with catch-all candidate measures on 11-point scales (likeability feeling thermometer, vote propensity, honesty, competence, charisma, assertiveness, left-right placement and absolute ideological proximity). Group comparisons: Cohen's d for male vs female prompt (Study 3) and Trump vs Merkel means (Study 4), plus sociodemographic means (Table A3). PCA reported with orthogonal varimax rotation for the prototype and candidate composites (Figures A4, A7).

findings.finding: The framework has 15 politically relevant personality facets (e.g., Trust & Faith in Others; Compromise & Cooperativeness; Assertiveness & Will to take control; Dedication & Sacrifice), each mapped to HEXACO, Big Five, VIA, Agency/Communion, and the Aaldering and Vliegenthart (2016) traits.
findings.numbers: 15 facets; 4-item scales plus one 2-item scale (Dedication & Sacrifice)

findings.finding: Self-rated facet reliabilities (Study 2) were moderate to high for most facets but low for several.
findings.numbers: alpha .44-.87; omega .43-.84. Lowest: Loyalty to Principles alpha .44 / omega .46; Humility alpha .46 / omega .43; Compromise alpha .51 / omega .45. Highest: Dedication alpha .87 / omega .84 (2-item scale)

findings.finding: Self-rated facets converge with the expected Big Five domains in the BFI-2-XS (Study 2): trust, compromise and empathy track Agreeableness; passion tracks Extraversion; optimism and composure track Emotional Stability.
findings.numbers: Trust-A r = .50; Empathy-A r = .48; Compromise-A r = .33; Passion-E r = .57; Optimism-ES r = .63; Self-Confidence-ES r = .56; Manners-C r = .59; Creativity-O r = .33. Machiavellianism: Integrity r = -.44, Empathy r = -.44, Humility r = -.37

findings.finding: Intellect & Mental Acuity correlated unexpectedly with BFI-2 Emotional Stability, mostly driven by one depression item.
Essential unidimensionality for most facets in self-ratings, with Creativity & Problem-Solving the clear exception and Loyalty to Principles borderline.
findings.numbers: Horn parallel analysis retained one component for all facets except Creativity; 15 scales judged essentially unidimensional

findings.finding: Ideal-politician prototypes showed almost no dependence on the politician's gender. Only Assertiveness differed, and it was rated more desirable for a female politician.
findings.location: Study 3 results, p.28; Table A5, p.74
findings.numbers: |d| = .00-.19; Assertiveness d = .19, p = .025 (male N = 289, female N = 300)

related.why: Same author group. Birkenmaier & Lechner operationalize two PoliPers facets (Assertiveness/Agency and Empathy/Communion) as text cues, and that is the version the system's codebook ports.
Expert ratings of US senators are the system's gold panel. PoliPers shows that citizen observer ratings carry ideological-proximity bias, which motivates checking the panel for the same.
Ramey infers domain-level Big Five from speech. PoliPers argues domain-level measures lack political contextualization and favors facet-level, role-specific items.
Hierarchical facet-level inventory construction. PoliPers validates against the short BFI-2-XS version of this instrument.
The BFI-2-XS is the convergent-validity instrument in PoliPers Study 2 (the paper cites the 2018 German version).
PoliPers cites Amsalem et al. on politicians' personality and media visibility (lower A, higher E/ES/O more covered).

Byrne supplies the pressure mechanism the receptivity layer assumes. PoliPers supplies facet definitions but no pressure-response evidence, so the two together show the gap between construct and engine use.
